facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: OGHONM 1000th Episode: The Q&A From the Live Recording
facts.name: Sinead O'Connor

facts.title: Major Label Control (1987)
facts.body: Despite her young age of 20 and being seven months pregnant, Sinéad O'Connor was uniquely allowed to self-facilitate and self-produce her debut album for a major label, an unprecedented degree of power and control. "Nobody at that age was given that kind of power and control for a major label release, but Shaneid got it."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Sinead O'Connor

facts.title: Increased Guitar Use (By 1987)
facts.body: By 1987, guitars became much more commonly used in industrial music, especially by North American groups such as Skinny Puppy and Ministry, indicating a shift in the genre's sonic palette. "By 1987, it was very clear that things were changing rapidly on the industrial scene. Thanks to groups like Skinny Puppy and Ministry, guitars were being used a lot more, especially by North American industrial groups."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Industrial

facts.title: Lindsey Buckingham's Departure in 1987
facts.body: Toward the end of 1987, Lindsey Buckingham unexpectedly announced his departure from Fleetwood Mac, just weeks before the launch of a tour to support "Tango in the Night." This decision stemmed from his burnout after carrying the creative burden of the latest LP. "Toward the end of 1987, Buckingham stunned his fellow bandmates when, just weeks before the launch of a tour to support Tango, he announced he was leaving Fleetwood Mac, the result of his burnout after carrying their latest LP."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.name: Fleetwood Mac

facts.title: Denver Radio Station Hostage Standoff – Fan Demanded All-Smiths Playlist at Gunpoint (1987)
facts.body: In 1987, a young man walked into a Denver radio station and took over the control room at gunpoint, demanding that the station stop playing mainstream rock and broadcast exclusively The Smiths. The standoff lasted four solid hours — four hours of uninterrupted Smiths — before a SWAT team negotiator talked him into surrendering. The man appeared to be acting out some kind of doomed romantic, idealistic gesture. "With his gun, [he] took over the control room of the radio station for four solid hours. And during that time, it was all Smiths all the time."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Smiths

facts.title: Breakup Announcement (September 12, 1987)
facts.body: Internal conflicts, including personality clashes, drug use, and disputes with their record label, led to the inevitable breakup of The Smiths. Rumors circulated in the British press throughout the spring of 1987, and on August 18, 1987, singer Morrissey informed producer Steven Street of his intention to leave for a solo career. The official public announcement of the band's dissolution came on September 12, 1987, a traumatic event for hardcore fans who deeply connected with the band's music, comparable in impact to the Beatles' 1970 breakup for a specific generation. "On August 18th, 1987, Morrissey, the singer, sent a letter to Smith's producer, Steven Street, telling him that he intended to break up the band so we could pursue a solo career."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 6
facts.name: The Smiths

facts.title: Band Breakup (1987)
facts.body: The band "exploded" in the fall of 1987, leading to the members pursuing individual careers shortly thereafter. "The Smiths exploded in the fall of 1987 and just months later, Morrissey appears as a solo artist."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Smiths

facts.title: Official Breakup (September 12, 1987)
facts.body: After recording their final studio album, "Strangeways, Here We Come," The Smiths officially broke up on September 12, 1987. Their mystery and influence, however, have endured despite their short career. "The album came out on May 19, 1987. And on September 12 of that year, it was official. The Smiths had broken up."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Smiths
facts.name: The Smiths

facts.title: Named After Desert Tree
facts.body: This album was originally conceived under the working title "Desert Song." Just before Christmas in 1986, U2, accompanied by photographer Anton Corbijn, traveled to the Mojave Desert to shoot photos for the album. During discussions on day one of the shoot, Corbijn and Bono talked about Joshua trees and their mythology, leading Bono to suggest naming the new record *The Joshua Tree*. The album's iconic cover features a photograph of a solitary Joshua tree. "Bono suggested that the new record be called the Joshua Tree."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Alt Rock Shrines ｜ From the Archives
facts.name: Joshua Tree

facts.title: Biggest U2 Record
facts.body: Produced in 1987, this album is identified as the biggest U2 record of them all and was produced by Daniel Lanois. "1987's The Joshua Tree."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Joshua Tree

facts.body: A key theme for "The Joshua Tree," hinted at by the original title "Two Americas," arose from the band's extensive touring in the United States in the years prior to the album. During this period, U2 connected with American artists like Bob Dylan and deepened their relationship with European artists such as The Rolling Stones, who were deeply enamored with American culture and music. This exposure led Bono to feel U2 lacked musical roots, prompting the band to study and integrate classic American music, including Country, Blues, and classic American Rock, drawing inspiration from early electric guitars influenced by Chuck Berry. Beyond music, Bono immersed himself in classic American literature and observed the social and cultural aspects, particularly the "breakdown of the American Dream," which became a significant source of inspiration for the album's themes. "tenemos muchas influencias del Country, tenemos muchas influencias del blues, tenemos muchas influencias del rock clásico americano, incluso de las primeras guitarras eléctricas en Chuck Berry."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.name: Joshua Tree

facts.body: Before its release, the album was expected to be very good, but it far exceeded expectations by selling beyond 25 million copies. It is now regarded as one of the most significant rock releases of all time, transforming into a cultural phenomenon with an impact lasting for years, even decades. "This is beyond just lightening in a bottle."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: U2 and The Joshua Tree at 30 with Daniel Lanois Part 2
facts.name: Joshua Tree

facts.body: Brian Eno enlisted Mark Price (known as Flood), a highly regarded engineer, to assist with this album. Flood's involvement highlights his growing reputation in the music industry during the late 1980s. "But then a couple of years his work was so highly regarded that Brian Eno asked him to help out you too on the Joshua Tree album."

facts.body: By the time of this album's release, U2 had successfully assimilated the lessons learned from observing Bruce Springsteen's live performances and songwriting methodology, particularly how to magnify the emotional impact of their songs in large stadium settings. This absorption of influence was instrumental in their eventual ascent to become one of the biggest bands globally. "And by the time they get to the Joshua Tree in 1987, you too had figured out what Springsteen was doing."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Joshua Tree

facts.body: During the recording of "The Joshua Tree" album, U2 had an abundance of songs. Although some tracks like "The Sweetest Thing" were written around this time, they didn't make the final album cut but found a home on singles from the album. "You too was on such a role when they recorded the Joshua tree album. They had more songs than they knew what to do with."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.body: For "The Joshua Tree" and subsequent albums, U2 significantly refined their composition methods. Previously, the band would enter recording sessions with songs still creatively "raw" and sometimes with unfinished lyrics, completing the composition process during recording. With "The Joshua Tree," Bono began to treat lyric writing almost like poetry, working on them in isolation with a highly literary approach. The rest of the band would then compose the music based on these nearly completed lyrics. This more complex and professional method differed greatly from the approach U2 used in their earlier albums. "Bono empieza a trabajar las letras casi como poemas, a escribir las ensolitario, a trabajar las de manera completamente literaria, mientras que la banda después con unas letras casi terminadas empieza a trabajar en la composición de la música."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.name: Joshua Tree

facts.body: Produced in 1987, this album is identified as the biggest U2 record of them all and was produced by Daniel Lanois. "1987's The Joshua Tree."

facts.body: Ranked among the best-selling albums ever, *The Joshua Tree* is lauded for its opening track, "Where the Streets Have No Name," featuring a brilliant, cinematic introduction that develops over nearly two minutes before Bono's vocals begin. "One of the best selling albums of all time is the Joshua Tree from YouTube."

facts.body: Released on March 9, 1987, this album is U2's fifth and has sold over 25 million copies, establishing it as one of the best-selling albums of all time. It reached number one in two dozen countries, and five of its eleven songs were released as singles, with several selling over a million copies. The supporting tour expanded from arenas to stadiums, leading to the live record "Live from Paris" and the documentary film "Rattle and Hum." The album earned U2 two Grammys: Album of the Year and Group of the Year, solidifying their status as one of the biggest bands globally. In 2014, it was added to the US Library of Congress for its cultural, historical, and aesthetic significance. "The Joshua Tree set up the band as one of the biggest in the world, and over the coming decade, they would become the biggest band in the world."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: U2 and The Joshua Tree at 30 with Daniel Lanois Part 1
facts.name: Joshua Tree

facts.body: The album marked a turning point for U2, with its political content becoming increasingly explicit. The band was deeply affected by various late 1980s events, including the Civil War in El Salvador, the plight of mothers in South America who had lost children in civil wars and dictatorships, mining strikes in the United Kingdom, and the persistent religious terrorism in Northern Ireland. These events provided a rich tapestry for the album's direct political commentary, which became a defining feature of "The Joshua Tree" and subsequent U2 albums. "tenemos la Guerra Civil del Salvador, tenemos las famosas comadronas en su América, que habían perdido a sus hijos en las trasitadulas y las guerras civiles, tenemos las vulgas de la minería en el Reconido, tenemos las continuas duchas todavía el terrorismo religioso que había en Irlanda del Norte, y eso viene a ser un poco la guinda del pastel."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.name: Joshua Tree

facts.body: The album was not originally intended to be called "The Joshua Tree". Its initial proposed titles were "The Desert Songs" and later "Two Americas". The final name change occurred when the band went to the Mojave Desert in California, specifically Joshua Tree National Park, for the album's cover photography. The iconic Joshua Tree photographed for the cover still stands there today, marked with a commemorative plaque. The discarded original titles, "The Desert Songs" and "Two Americas," better hint at the album's thematic content. "Finalmente se terminó cambiando del Yosu Atri cuando la banda fue a hacerse las fotografías para la portada y para todo el árbol del disco, eso fueron al desierto de Mojave, en California, al Parque Nacional de Yosu."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.name: Joshua Tree

facts.body: The album was produced by the highly influential Brian Eno and his personal friend Daniel Lanois. Brian Eno had previously produced several U2 albums and continued to work with them afterwards, with Bono attributing much of U2's success to Eno's significant production work. Both producers took an unconventional approach, not only handling classic production duties but also playing instruments and contributing backing vocals on some songs during the recording of "The Joshua Tree." "tanto, Brian Nino como Daniel Lanois, a trabajar durante el álbum no solo en trabajos de producción, sino que tocaron instrumentos durante la grabación del álbum, pero incluso a sus voces figuran en los coros algunas de las canciones."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.name: Joshua Tree

facts.body: The album's working title "The Desert Songs" alludes to its spiritual journey theme, which sparked ongoing debate about its Christian or religious connotations. During this period, Bono embarked on a significant spiritual process, blending humanitarian efforts (such as his trips to Africa to raise money) with mystical and religious experiences. This led to themes of inner exploration, self-discovery, and human morality throughout the album, with numerous references to God, faith, and spiritual seeking. These elements, combined with the "Joshua Tree" imagery, contribute to the album's ambiguous but evident spiritual and potentially Christian undertones. "Bono comenzó un enorme fase de proceso espiritual durante esta época, de hecho, cuando le empezó a hacer sus viajes a África, a conocer las abrones de África, lluchar por este tipo de causas, a recalar dinero."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.name: Joshua Tree

facts.body: This album marks its 30th anniversary this week since its publication in 1987. It was the third consecutive album for U2 to receive maximum critical acclaim and remains the band's best-selling album to date, with approximately 28 million copies sold. It holds the 26th position on Rolling Stone magazine's list of the greatest albums in history. In 1987, it earned U2 their first Grammy for Best Album of the Year and quickly rose to number one on sales charts. Curiously, it also positioned at number 36 on the list of best Christian albums in 1987. The album was recorded rapidly, taking only three months despite its high quality. During its creation, U2 began refining their composition methods, moving towards a more structured approach where Bono would work on lyrics as poems, and the band would then compose the music with almost finished texts. The band's positive mood following the success of their previous three albums also contributed to this process. "Al día de hoy, ha vendido unos 28 millones de copias y sigue siendo el álbum más vendido de la banda U2."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan

facts.body: This album was originally conceived under the working title "Desert Song." Just before Christmas in 1986, U2, accompanied by photographer Anton Corbijn, traveled to the Mojave Desert to shoot photos for the album. During discussions on day one of the shoot, Corbijn and Bono talked about Joshua trees and their mythology, leading Bono to suggest naming the new record *The Joshua Tree*. The album's iconic cover features a photograph of a solitary Joshua tree. "Bono suggested that the new record be called the Joshua Tree."

facts.title: American Influences
facts.body: A key theme for "The Joshua Tree," hinted at by the original title "Two Americas," arose from the band's extensive touring in the United States in the years prior to the album. During this period, U2 connected with American artists like Bob Dylan and deepened their relationship with European artists such as The Rolling Stones, who were deeply enamored with American culture and music. This exposure led Bono to feel U2 lacked musical roots, prompting the band to study and integrate classic American music, including Country, Blues, and classic American Rock, drawing inspiration from early electric guitars influenced by Chuck Berry. Beyond music, Bono immersed himself in classic American literature and observed the social and cultural aspects, particularly the "breakdown of the American Dream," which became a significant source of inspiration for the album's themes. "tenemos muchas influencias del Country, tenemos muchas influencias del blues, tenemos muchas influencias del rock clásico americano, incluso de las primeras guitarras eléctricas en Chuck Berry."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan

facts.title: Nikki Sixx's 1987 Overdose
facts.body: On December 23, 1987, Mötley Crüe bassist Nikki Sixx experienced a severe overdose. His heart stopped, and he was clinically dead for two minutes, requiring two shots of adrenaline to be revived. "Nikki Sixth of Motley Crew needed two shots of adrenaline to restart his heart on December 23rd, 1987. He was gone for two minutes."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Roots of Modern Gothic Music (1987)
facts.body: The Sisters of Mercy, specifically with a song from 1987, are used to illustrate the historical lineage of modern gothic music. The roots of this compositional style are traced back over 800 years to Hildegard von Bingen's sacred monophony, composed around 1156, and its suitability for performance in massive stone cathedrals. "Yes, that's the systems of mercy from 1987, but the roots of that kind of composition go back to 1156."

The roots of this compositional style are traced back over 800 years to Hildegard von Bingen's sacred monophony, composed around 1156, and its suitability for performance in massive stone cathedrals. "Yes, that's the systems of mercy from 1987, but the roots of that kind of composition go back to 1156."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Sisters of Mercy

facts.title: R.E.M.'s Multinational Era (Post-1987)
facts.body: R.E.M. transitioned to Warner Music after experiencing "problems and certain disagreements" with their previous independent label, IRS Records, around 1987. From this point forward, R.E.M. consistently remained with multinational labels, releasing what many consider their "great trilogy" of albums, which are revered as some of the finest in US music history. "se pasaría a Warner y a partir de ahí rem estaría siempre multinacionales."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: El papel de REM en los '80
facts.name: Warner

facts.title: Trademark Kangol Hat (1987)
facts.body: LL Cool J's "trademark Kangol hat" was famously targeted in the artwork for Cool Mo Dee's 1987 album "How Ya Like Me Now," which depicted a Jeep crushing it as part of their lyrical beef. This visual diss became an iconic image in rap history. "whose cover depicted a Jeep crushing LL's trademark can goal hat"
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

facts.title: Role in Nike "Revolution" Deal (1987)
facts.body: Yoko Ono helped broker the deal for The Beatles' song "Revolution" to be used in a 1987 Nike commercial. Her involvement was driven by the belief that this commercial exposure would introduce her late husband John Lennon's music to a new generation of fans. "She helped broker the deal because she thought it would help bring her late husband's music to a new generation of fans."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Concept of Selling Out: Part 1
facts.name: Yoko Ono

facts.title: Late Night with David Letterman Reunion (1987)
facts.body: On November 13, 1987, Sonny and Cher reunited on "Late Night with David Letterman," holding hands and singing their classic hit "I Got You Babe," an event that captivated audiences. "So I was watching late night with David Letterman on November 13, 1987, when Sunny and Share reunited, and then they held hands and they sang, I got you, babe, the very epitome of a pop song."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 34 - A 70s Pop Manifesto - Finding Meaning in 70s Pop
facts.name: Sonny & Cher
